rows.recommendation: Based on one trial, use of the microaxial flow pump in selected patients with cardiogenic shock related to acute myocardial infarction is reasonable to reduce death. However, complications such as bleeding, limb ischemia, and renal failure are higher with the microaxial flow pump compared with usual care. Therefore, careful attention to vascular access and weaning of support is important to appropriately balance the benefits and risks.
Red blood cell transfusion to maintain a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL may be reasonable in patients with ACS and acute or chronic anemia who are not actively bleeding.

After discharge, focus on secondary prevention is fundamental. A fasting lipid panel is recommended 4 to 8 weeks after initiating or adjusting the dose of lipid-lowering therapy. Referral to cardiac rehabilitation is also recommended, with the option for home-based programs for patients unable or unwilling to attend in person.

content.narrative_summary: Section 2.1 defines acute coronary syndromes (ACS) as disruption of unstable coronary artery atherosclerotic plaque leading to thrombosis or microemboli, causing myocardial ischemia. It describes the continuum of clinical conditions—unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI—based on ECG findings and troponin biomarkers, and notes dynamic progression among these states. Less common causes of myocardial ischemia (spasm, embolism, dissection) are mentioned. The guideline’s focus on acute management of ACS under the Universal Definition of MI is introduced, with reference to separate evaluations for type 2 MI, spontaneous dissections, and MINOCA, and an external chest pain guideline.

content.narrative_summary: The page presents Figure 1 illustrating the pathobiology of a type 1 myocardial infarction due to atherosclerotic plaque disruption, emphasizing lipid accumulation, plaque instability, rupture, thrombus formation, and resulting myocardial ischemia and myonecrosis. The narrative expands on these mechanisms, highlights the importance of early therapy in patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACS), notes that cardiovascular risk remains elevated for months to years after an ACS event due to a persistent inflammatory milieu, and references extended management strategies aligned with chronic coronary disease guidelines.

figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Progressive lipid accumulation and inflammation within an atherosclerotic plaque may lead to plaque instability. Rupture or erosion of the atherosclerotic plaque and exposure of plaque contents to the circulation may then culminate in activation of the coagulation cascade and subsequent thrombosis. When this occurs in the epicardial vessels of the coronary circulation, the presence of thrombus may compromise flow to the myocardium, leading to myocardial ischemia and eventual myonecrosis. figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Columns: "Electrocardiographic evidence of ischemia," "NSTE-ACS," and "STEMI." Row 1 (evidence of ischemia): NSTE-ACS: new or presumed new dynamic horizontal or down-sloping ST-segment depression ≥0.5 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads and/or T-wave inversion ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads with prominent R wave or R/S ratio ≥1 or transient ST-segment elevation. STEMI: new or presumed new ST-segment elevation of ≥1 mm in ≥2 anatomically contiguous leads (measured at the J-point) in leads other than V2–V3 and ≥2 mm in men ≥40 y, ≥2.5 mm in men <40 y, and ≥1.5 mm in women regardless of age in leads V2–V3.* Row 2 (other observed changes): NSTE-ACS: nonspecific ST-segment or T-wave changes or a normal ECG; absence of ischemic changes does not exclude ACS. STEMI: posterior leads (V7–V9) should be obtained in suspected left circumflex occlusion with isolated ST-segment depression ≥0.5 mm in leads V1–V3. Footnotes note mimics and exclusions.

section_headings: 3. INITIAL EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT OF SUSPECTED ACS
3.1.1. Prehospital Assessment and Management Considerations for Suspected ACS
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis emphasizes the importance of rapid, coordinated prehospital care and EMS transport in the optimal management of suspected ACS, noting advantages over private vehicle transport for assessment, monitoring, and treatment of life-threatening conditions. It also highlights that trained prehospital personnel should obtain a focused assessment in patients with suspected ACS.

recommendation_tables.title: Suspected ACS

rows.recommendation: In patients with suspected ACS, a 12-lead ECG should be acquired and interpreted within 10 minutes of first medical contact (FMC)* to identify patients with STEMI.

In patients with suspected ACS in which the initial ECG is nondiagnostic of STEMI, serial ECGs to detect potential ischemic changes should be performed, especially when clinical suspicion of ACS is high, symptoms are persistent, or the clinical condition deteriorates.

recommendation_tables.title: STEMI

rows.recommendation: In patients with suspected STEMI, immediate emergency medical services (EMS) transport to a PCI-capable hospital for primary PCI (PPCI‡) is the recommended triage strategy, with an FMC-to-first-device time system goal of ≤90 minutes.

In patients with suspected STEMI, early advance notification of the receiving PCI-capable hospital by EMS personnel and activation of the cardiac catheterization team is recommended to reduce time to reperfusion.

section_headings: 3.1.2. Initial In-Hospital Assessment of Patients With Confirmed or Suspected ACS
content.narrative_summary: This page outlines initial in-hospital assessment for patients with confirmed or suspected ACS, highlighting rapid ECG acquisition and interpretation within 10 minutes, serial ECGs if the initial tracing is nondiagnostic, prompt measurement of cardiac troponin (preferably high-sensitivity assays), and specified intervals for repeat troponin testing. The accompanying narrative emphasizes focused history and rapid evaluation, the role of echocardiography for hemodynamic or mechanical complication assessment, clinical decision pathways to optimize resource use, and considerations for identifying STEMI and NSTE-ACS findings on ECG.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Initial In-Hospital Assessment of Patients With Confirmed or Suspected ACS

rows.recommendation: In patients with suspected ACS, acquisition and interpretation of an ECG within 10 minutes is recommended to help guide patient management.*1,2

In patients with suspected ACS in whom the initial ECG is nondiagnostic, serial 12-lead ECGs should be performed to detect potential ischemic changes, especially when clinical suspicion of ACS is high, symptoms are persistent, or clinical condition deteriorates.*3
In patients with suspected ACS, cTn should be measured as soon as possible, preferably using a high-sensitivity cTn (hs-cTn) assay.*4-7

In patients with suspected ACS with an initial hs-cTn or cTn that is nondiagnostic, the recommended time intervals for repeat measurements after the initial sample collection (time zero) are 1 to 2 hours for hs-cTn and 3 to 6 hours for conventional cTn assays.*8-12

section_headings: 3.2 Management of Patients Presenting With Cardiac Arrest
content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis notes that ~10% of STEMI patients transferred by EMS have out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, emphasizing early recognition and direct transfer to PCI-capable centers to improve survival; outcomes are <10% to discharge in comatose patients regardless of etiology, with improved survival if witnessed arrest and shockable rhythm. Patients with return of spontaneous circulation and ST-elevation who are awake on ECG are candidates for PPCI, whereas stable patients without ST-elevation after arrest may defer immediate angiography pending risk stratification. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text begins describing observational data from the CARES registry linking transfer to PCI-capable centers with improved survival but is cut off mid-sentence.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Patients Presenting With Cardiac Arrest

rows.recommendation: Patients with cardiac arrest and STEMI who have been resuscitated should preferentially be transferred by EMS to a PPCI-capable center.

Patients who have been resuscitated after cardiac arrest and are noncomatose or who are comatose with favorable prognostic features and with evidence of STEMI, should undergo PPCI to improve survival.
In patients with cardiac arrest who are comatose, have unfavorable prognostic features, and evidence of STEMI, PPCI may be reasonable after individualized assessment.

In resuscitated patients who are comatose after cardiac arrest, electrically and hemodynamically stable, and without evidence of STEMI, immediate angiography is not recommended due to lack of benefit.

content.narrative_summary: Aspirin is a key antiplatelet therapy in ACS, reducing vascular death and MACE. The guideline recommends an initial loading dose (162–325 mg) followed by daily low-dose aspirin (75–100 mg). If oral administration is not feasible, rectal or intravenous routes may be used. Aspirin discontinuation strategies after 1–3 months may be considered to lower bleeding risk, and desensitization is preferred for those with hypersensitivity to enable dual antiplatelet therapy. The use of P2Y12 inhibitors is recommended regardless of aspirin hypersensitivity history.

section_headings: Recommendations for Oral P2Y12 Inhibitors During Hospitalization

In-Hospital Management in Patients With NSTE-ACS

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes that oral P2Y12 receptor antagonists inhibit adenosine diphosphate–mediated platelet activation. Adding a P2Y12 inhibitor to aspirin across the ACS spectrum reduces platelet aggregation and recurrent MACE but increases bleeding risk. Patients with ACS should receive a loading dose followed by daily dosing, with choice of agent based on management strategy and bleeding risk. Available oral P2Y12 inhibitors include clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticagrelor. Clopidogrel is least potent, requires hepatic bioactivation, and exhibits pharmacodynamic variability, placing hyporesponders at higher risk of MACE and stent thrombosis after PCI. Ticagrelor ...

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Oral P2Y12 Inhibitors During Hospitalization

rows.recommendation: In patients with ACS, an oral P2Y12 inhibitor should be administered in addition to aspirin to reduce MACE.^1-5
In patients with a history of stroke or transient ischemic attack, prasugrel should not be administered because of worse net clinical outcomes.*14
In patients with NSTE-ACS undergoing PCI, prasugrel or ticagrelor is recommended to reduce MACE and stent thrombosis.^4-6
In patients with NSTE-ACS who are managed without planned invasive evaluation, ticagrelor is recommended to reduce MACE.^5,7
In patients with NSTE-ACS, clopidogrel is recommended to reduce MACE when prasugrel or ticagrelor are unavailable, cannot be tolerated, or are contraindicated.^1

In patients with NSTE-ACS planned for an invasive strategy with timing of angiography anticipated to be >24 hours, upstream treatment with clopidogrel or ticagrelor may be considered to reduce MACE.^1,5,8
In patients with STEMI managed with PPCI, prasugrel or ticagrelor should be administered to reduce MACE and stent thrombosis.^4,5,9,10
In patients with STEMI managed with PPCI, clopidogrel is recommended to reduce MACE and stent thrombosis when prasugrel or ticagrelor are unavailable, cannot be tolerated, or are contraindicated.^11
In patients with STEMI managed with fibrinolytic therapy, clopidogrel should be administered concurrently to reduce death and MACE.^2,3

content.narrative_summary: This page continues the discussion of antithrombotic therapy in acute coronary syndrome, reviewing trial data on bivalirudin in NSTE-ACS and presenting recommendations 7–11 on the use of parenteral anticoagulants including enoxaparin and fondaparinux during primary PCI and in fibrinolytic-treated STEMI, with attention to ischemic outcomes and bleeding risk from key trials (ACUITY, MATRIX, ATOLL, OASIS-5/6, ExTRACT-TIMI 25, GUSTO, ASSENT-3).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations 7–11

rows.recommendation: Intravenous enoxaparin compared with UFH reduces the risk for ischemic outcomes without a significant difference in bleeding in the setting of PPCI.
rows.supporting_text: In the ATOLL (Acute Myocardial Infarction Treated with Primary Angioplasty and Intravenous Enoxaparin or Unfractionated Heparin to Lower Ischemic and Bleeding Events at Short- and Long-term Follow-up) trial, which enrolled patients presenting with STEMI, the primary endpoint of 30-day incidence of death, complication of MI, procedural failure, or major bleeding occurred in 28% of patients with enoxaparin compared with 34% with UFH (P = 0.06). Although the incidence of primary endpoint was not significantly different between enoxaparin and UFH, the secondary endpoint of 30-day death, recurrent ACS, or urgent revascularization was significantly lower in the enoxaparin group (7% versus 11%; P = 0.015). In addition, a net clinical benefit (death, complication of MI, or major bleeding) was observed with enoxaparin compared with UFH (10% versus 15%; P = 0.03). In a meta-analysis of 10,451 patients, intravenous enoxaparin was associated with a significant reduction in death and major bleeding.

rows.recommendation: Fondaparinux should not be used as the sole anticoagulant to support PCI because of the risk of catheter thrombosis.
rows.supporting_text: In the OASIS-5 trial, an increase was observed in the rate of catheter-related thrombus with fondaparinux compared with enoxaparin (0.9% versus 0.4%). Similar results were observed in the OASIS-6 (The Safety and Efficacy of Fondaparinux versus Control Therapy in Patients with STEMI) trial in which a higher rate of guiding-catheter thrombosis and more coronary complications with fondaparinux were observed when used during PCI.

rows.recommendation: In patients with STEMI treated with fibrinolytic therapy, parenteral anticoagulation is recommended before and after fibrinolytic therapy to reduce ischemic events.
rows.supporting_text: In studies of fibrinolytic therapy such as the GUSTO (Global Utilization of Streptokinase and Tissue Plasminogen Activator for Occluded Coronary Arteries) trial, the ASSENT-3 (Assessment of the Safety and Efficacy of a New Thrombolytic Regimen) trial, or the ExTRACT-TIMI 25 (Enoxaparin and Thrombolysis Reperfusion for Acute Myocardial Infarction Treatment-Thrombolysis In Myocardial Infarction 25) study, intravenous heparin was administered for at least 48 hours. In the ExTRACT-TIMI 25 study, the UFH infusion was given for at least 48 hours but could be continued for a longer period at the treating physician’s discretion, whereas the subcutaneous injections of enoxaparin were continued until hospital discharge or for a maximum of 8 days (whichever came first). Patients randomized to enoxaparin had a lower risk of death or nonfatal recurrent MI through 30 days compared with UFH (9.9% versus 12.0%); however, treatment with enoxaparin was associated with an increase in major bleeding (2.1% versus 1.4%).

rows.recommendation: In patients with STEMI who received fibrinolytic therapy and who are not planned for an invasive approach, enoxaparin is the preferred anticoagulant over UFH.
rows.supporting_text: In the ExTRACT-TIMI 25 study, enoxaparin until hospital discharge or for a maximum of 8 days (whichever came first) was compared with UFH administered for at least 48 hours (could be continued for a longer period at the treating physician’s discretion) in 20,506 patients with STEMI receiving fibrinolytic therapy. The primary endpoint of death or nonfatal recurrent MI through 30 days occurred in 12% in the UFH group compared with 9.9% in the enoxaparin group. In a meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials, UFH did not reduce reinfarction or death in patients treated with fibrinolytic therapy. In contrast, low-molecular-weight heparin reduced the risk of reinfarction and death compared with placebo and the risk of reinfarction.

rows.recommendation: In patients with STEMI who are not likely to undergo an invasive approach, fondaparinux is an alternate anticoagulant that can be used.
rows.supporting_text: In the OASIS-6 trial of patients with STEMI who were treated with thrombolytic agents (predominantly streptokinase), fondaparinux significantly reduced the risk of the primary endpoint of death or reinfarction at 30 days, including a significant reduction in mortality, reinfarction, and severe bleeding when compared with placebo or UFH.

content.title: 4.5 Lipid Management
content.narrative_summary: Randomized controlled trials support more aggressive LDL-C targets after ACS, demonstrating event reduction proportional to LDL-C lowering. High-intensity statins reduce LDL-C and major adverse cardiovascular events by ≈15%. For those not at goal or intolerant to statins, nonstatin therapies—including ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, and bempedoic acid—further lower LDL-C and improve outcomes. A lipid profile is recommended as soon as feasible after ACS presentation, and post-discharge lipid management is discussed in Section 11.2.

content.title: 4.7. Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System Inhibitors
content.narrative_summary: Oral ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) reduce all-cause death and MACE in patients with STEMI or NSTEMI, particularly those with high-risk features such as LVEF ≤40%, hypertension, diabetes, or anterior STEMI. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists confer additional mortality and MACE reduction in ACS patients with reduced LVEF and HF symptoms or diabetes. Sacubitril-valsartan appears safe when initiated early after MI for HF with reduced ejection fraction. Randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate survival and MACE benefits with these agents.

section_headings: 5.3.1 Timing and Choice of Agent for Fibrinolytic Therapy
content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses the preference for primary PCI when feasible; when not possible, fibrinolytic therapy in STEMI patients provides a time-dependent mortality and morbidity reduction within 12 hours of symptom onset, especially in early presenters with low bleeding risk and large anterior infarctions. Fibrin-specific agents (tenecteplase, reteplase, alteplase) are preferred due to superior potency and lower immunogenicity. Tenecteplase is genetically engineered with higher fibrin specificity and equivalent 30-day mortality to alteplase but less noncerebral bleeding. Adjunctive antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapies apply regardless of fibrinolytic choice. Patients should be transferred to PCI-capable hospitals after fibrinolysis for routine coronary angiography, and failed reperfusion signs are addressed in Section 5.3.2.

6.1. Rationale and Timing for a Routine Invasive or Selective Invasive Approach
content.narrative_summary: Contemporary data show that a pharmaco-invasive strategy (lysis followed by PCI ≥2 hours later) reduces mortality by ~21% versus fibrinolysis alone, with similar bleeding rates even when catheterization is very early. Optimal timing of angiography post-fibrinolysis remains undefined. A routine invasive approach involves coronary angiography with intent to perform PCI or CABG in NSTE-ACS, providing prognostic information and reducing MACE compared to a selective invasive approach. Evidence derives from RCTs conducted before hs-cTn assays, radial access, newer drug-eluting stents, and modern antiplatelets. High-risk patients typically benefit from routine invasive management, whereas low-risk or biomarker-negative patients may undergo selective invasive evaluation.

content.title: 7.3. Use of Intracoronary Imaging
content.narrative_summary: Intracoronary imaging serves as a valuable tool for guiding the placement of coronary stents, particularly in left main artery or complex lesions, by using IVUS and OCT to assess plaque burden, lesion length, vessel dimensions, and stent apposition. Both modalities improve stent expansion, reduce malapposition and dissections, and aid in selecting stent size and deployment strategies, though they require contrast injection and have limited imaging depth. Randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that IVUS- or OCT-guided PCI lowers target vessel failure, cardiac death, target vessel myocardial infarction, ischemia-driven revascularization, and stent thrombosis, with OCT shown to be noninferior to IVUS for most outcomes.

rows.recommendation: In patients with ACS undergoing coronary stent implantation in left main artery or in complex lesions, intracoronary imaging with intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) or optical coherence tomography (OCT) is recommended for procedural guidance to reduce ischemic events.

7.4.1. Management of Multivessel CAD in STEMI
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis summarizes randomized trials demonstrating that in hemodynamically stable STEMI patients, multivessel PCI of nonculprit lesions reduces major adverse cardiovascular events and improves quality of life compared with culprit-only PCI, with lower recurrent ischemia when performed as a single procedure. Decision-making should consider clinical and hemodynamic status, lesion and infarct complexity, myocardium at risk, and comorbidities. Physiologic-guided versus angiographic-guided PCI approaches show no differential benefit. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text reviews key trials (e.g., PRAMI, COMPLETE) demonstrating significant reductions in MACE with complete revascularization strategies.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Multivessel CAD in STEMI

rows.recommendation: In selected, hemodynamically stable patients with STEMI and multivessel disease (MVD), after successful PCI of the infarct-related artery, PCI of significantly stenosed* noninfarct-related arteries is recommended to reduce the risk of death or MI and improve angina-related quality of life (QOL).†1-9

In appropriate patients with STEMI and complex MVD, after successful PCI of the infarct-related artery, elective CABG surgery for significantly stenosed noninfarct-related arteries involving the left anterior descending artery or left main disease is reasonable to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.†

In selected hemodynamically stable patients with STEMI and low-complexity MVD (those not intended for CABG surgery), multivessel PCI of significantly stenosed noninfarct-related arteries at the time of PPCI may be preferred over a staged approach to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.10-12

In patients with STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock, routine PCI of a noninfarct-related artery at the time of PPCI should not be performed because of the higher risk of death or renal failure.13-15

content.title: 9. ACS COMPLICATIONS / 9.1 Mechanical Complications
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis notes that timely reperfusion therapy has reduced mechanical complications of MI (ventricular septal rupture, mitral regurgitation, free wall rupture), which albeit sometimes incidental, can present with recurrent chest pain, new murmur, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or sudden death within the first week post-AMI. Medical therapy alone carries high early mortality; definitive surgical correction remains the treatment of choice, with highest mortality in cardiogenic shock or emergency intervention. Delaying surgery (>7 days) may lower mortality but carries risks; temporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices facilitate hemodynamic stabilization and end-organ recovery as a bridge to definitive repair. The recommendation-specific supportive text highlights no RCTs for transfer of post-MI mechanical complication patients to surgical centers; recommends transfer to Level 1 CICUs with multidisciplinary teams and MCS capability; emphasizes early corrective surgery with individualized MCS selection guided by patient characteristics and hemodynamics; and notes beneficial effects of IABP on shunting and use of MCS to permit delayed repair.

section_headings: 9.4. Management of LV Thrombus After MI
content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of post-MI complications, including high-degree atrioventricular block and indications for pacemaker insertion. Section 9.3 outlines diagnostic criteria for post-MI pericarditis (see Table 18) and describes early pericarditis presenting 1–3 days after transmural MI with inflammatory features, managed conservatively with acetaminophen. content.title: 10.5.3. Cardiac Rehabilitation
content.narrative_summary: Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a multifaceted and comprehensive outpatient intervention for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Its primary goals are modifying CVD risk factors, improving functional capacity and quality of life (QOL), and reducing morbidity and mortality. CR combines monitored exercise training, health and nutrition education, psychological support, and personalized patient assessment including medication optimization. It has been shown to lower cardiovascular and all-cause death, reduce hospital readmissions, and be cost-effective. Despite proven benefits, CR is underutilized, particularly among women and underrepresented groups, due to factors such as referral process gaps, communication issues, perceived inconvenience, and cost. To increase utilization, inpatient referral for ACS patients is recommended, and home-based CR programs should be considered for those in rural or center-limited settings, offering similar short-term safety and clinical outcomes as center-based programs.
